text:
*The first bite of the axe is the strangest part. Not pain exactly, but a wrongness. A cold notch where there has only ever been slow, patient growth.*

I've stood here for a hundred years. I remember when the clearing to my east was all saplings, and I watched them reach upward alongside me, one lean inch at a time. I've held a hundred springs of birdsong in my branches. Owls raised families in the hollow near my crown. Deer have napped in my shade, and once, decades ago, two children carved their initials into my bark. I healed around those letters. I kept them.

And now the chainsaw screams.

What do I feel? Bewilderment, mostly. I understand time in seasons and centuries. These men understand it in hours and paychecks. In twenty minutes they'll undo what took a hundred years to build. That math feels unbearably lopsided.

I feel the fungal threads beneath the soil trembling. My roots are tangled with my neighbors', and we've shared sugars and warnings through that network for generations. They'll feel me go. Some of them will be next.

But strangely, I'm not angry at the men themselves. One of them paused before he started, laid his hand flat against my trunk for just a moment. I felt it. Maybe he has a family to feed. Maybe he didn't choose this any more than I did.

So mostly I feel grief. Not for myself, but for what goes with me: the shade, the nests, the slow-built soil, the hundred years of quiet witnessing.

*And as I lean, as gravity finally wins, I let go of my last seeds into the wind. Just in case.*
